# Rules of Defeat: The First Rule of Defeat <note>original: Parajika Pali, Pathama Parajikam</note>

17. Furthermore, monks, a monk may be dissatisfied and discontented, wishing to leave the <term>samanna</term> <gloss>ascetic life</gloss>. Feeling distressed, ashamed, and disgusted with being a monk, he longs to be a layman <note>the text implies returning to the household life</note>... <note>omission in original</note> ...he longs for the state of not being a son of the Sakyans <note>referring to the followers of the Buddha, the Sakyamuni</note>. 

He says or makes it known: "I have a mother; she will support me." 
He says or makes it known: "I have a father; he will support me." 
He says or makes it known: "I have a brother; he will support me." 
He says or makes it known: "I have a sister; she will support me." 
He says or makes it known: "I have a son; he will support me." 
He says or makes it known: "I have a daughter; she will support me." 
He says or makes it known: "I have a wife; she will support me." 
He says or makes it known: "I have relatives; they will support me." 
He says or makes it known: "I have friends; they will support me." 
He says or makes it known: "I have a village; I will live by means of it." 
He says or makes it known: "I have a town; I will live by means of it." 
He says or makes it known: "I have a field; I will live by means of it." 
He says or makes it known: "I have property; I will live by means of it." 
He says or makes it known: "I have silver; I will live by means of it." 
He says or makes it known: "I have gold; I will live by means of it." 
... <note>omission in original</note> ... 
He says or makes it known: "I have a craft; I will live by means of it." 

In this way also, monks, there is an expression of weakness, yet the training is not renounced. <note>These statements alone do not constitute a formal resignation from the monastic order.</note>

18. Furthermore, monks, a monk may be dissatisfied and discontented, wishing to leave the ascetic life. Feeling distressed, ashamed, and disgusted with being a monk, he longs to be a layman... he longs for the state of not being a son of the Sakyans. 

He says or makes it known: "It is difficult to do." 
He says or makes it known: "It is not easy to do." 
He says or makes it known: "It is difficult to practice." 
He says or makes it known: "It is not easy to practice." 
He says or makes it known: "I cannot endure it." 
He says or makes it known: "I am not able." 
He says or makes it known: "I do not find delight." 
... <note>omission in original</note> ... 
He says or makes it known: "I find no satisfaction." 

In this way also, monks, there is an expression of weakness, yet the training is not renounced.

19. And how, monks, is there an expression of weakness and the training is renounced? In this case, monks, a monk is dissatisfied and discontented, wishing to leave the ascetic life. Feeling distressed, ashamed, and disgusted with being a monk, he longs to be a layman... he longs for the state of not being a son of the Sakyans. 

He says or makes it known: "I renounce the Buddha." 

In this way, monks, there is an expression of weakness and the training is renounced. <note>This specific declaration constitutes a formal departure from the monkhood.</note>

<summary>This page defines the difference between a monk merely expressing personal weakness or desire for worldly support and the formal renunciation of the Buddhist monastic training. The training is only considered officially broken when the monk explicitly renounces the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Sangha.</summary>
<keywords>Vinaya, monastic discipline, renunciation, Parajika, monkhood, Buddhist law</keywords>
